analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23 percent national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Tax Act would have wiped out the federal income tax, the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and replaced them with a single 23 percent national sales tax on almost everything people buy [S2]. It would have abolished the IRS by prohibiting its funding after fiscal year 2009, with states that already run sales taxes collecting the federal tax for a small fee [S2]. Every family would receive a monthly rebate covering the tax up to the poverty line [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 24, 2005 and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains go to the wealthiest households: the bill repeals the income tax on wages, capital gains, and dividends, and repeals the estate and gift tax entirely, while purchases made for investment, business, or export purposes are untaxed and used property is untaxed [S2][S3]. Workers benefit from the end of the 15.3 percent payroll tax that comes out of every paycheck [S2]. All families get a monthly rebate equal to the sales tax on the poverty-level amount for their household size [S3]. Anyone who hates filing tax returns benefits from abolishing the IRS and the income tax system [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax in their entirety [S2].
Imposes a single national sales tax set at 23 percent of gross payments in 2007, replacing all federal taxes on income [S2].
Gives every registered family a monthly rebate equal to the sales tax on the federal poverty level for their family size, paid through the Social Security Administration [S3].
Exempts purchases made for business, export, or investment purposes, and used property, from the tax [S2].
Abolishes the IRS by prohibiting its funding after fiscal year 2009 and hands primary collection of the federal tax to state governments for an administration fee [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend most or all of their income — typical working and middle-class families — would pay the 23 percent tax on nearly everything they buy, including rent, new goods, and services, with the rebate only covering spending up to the poverty line [S2][S3]. Because high-income households spend a smaller share of their income (and their investment, business, and used purchases are exempt), their effective tax rate would fall sharply [S3]. Future Congresses could also raise the rate: the bill sets a formula with adjustable rates after 2007 [S2]. Social Security and Medicare would be funded from general sales tax revenue rather than a dedicated payroll tax, ending the earmarked funding link [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes consumption at a flat rate but leaves investment purchases, business purchases, used property, and intangible wealth untaxed, so a household living entirely on existing wealth or asset appreciation could pay almost nothing, while a household spending its full paycheck pays the tax on everything it buys [S3].

The monthly rebate offsets the tax only up to the federal poverty level for a family's size; spending above that — rent, groceries beyond poverty-level budgets, utilities, clothing — is taxed at the full rate regardless of income [S3].

Repealing the payroll tax breaks the dedicated funding link for Social Security and Medicare; the bill instead directs the Treasury to allocate sales tax revenue among the trust funds, leaving benefits dependent on future sales tax collections [S2][S3].
The 23 percent rate applies only to 2007; the rate for later years is a formula that Congress could adjust, so the promise of a fixed low rate is not locked in [S2].

Families must file an annual registration with the sales tax authority, listing every member's Social Security number and certifying lawful residency, to keep receiving the rebate; missing the deadline suspends payments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's selling points — no income tax, no IRS, no tax filing — are real and would be felt by every household [S2]. But the trade is a tax cut concentrated on the wealthiest households (no income, capital gains, or estate tax; untaxed investment) paid for by a 23 percent tax on nearly everything working families buy, with only a poverty-level rebate as protection [S2][S3]. An honest supporter would acknowledge the distributional shift and the risk that the actual rate needed to replace current revenue would exceed the advertised 23 percent. The bill as written would move a substantial share of the federal tax burden from wealth onto wages and consumption.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chambliss introduced the bill in the Senate on January 24, 2005 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day — the only action the full Senate ever took on it [S5].
Only three senators cosponsored the bill, all Republicans [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No tax change occurred, so the existing income, payroll, and estate tax system stayed in place. Working households that would have paid a 23 percent tax on nearly all their spending, and large estates that would have escaped the estate tax had it become law, simply kept the current system instead. The outcome most clearly serves whoever preferred the status quo over a major tax rewrite.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The tax system stayed as it was

for.name: Sen. Saxby Chambliss
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2005 in the Senate and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 3 Senate Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the four supporters sat on the Finance Committee leadership.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a hearing, markup, or vote; the committee's file shows no action after the January 24, 2005 referral.

sides.party_line_note: No chamber ever voted on the bill, so no vote split exists; the only recorded support came from its four Republican sponsors and cosponsors, and the Finance Committee — chaired by a Republican — let it sit without action.

industries.note: The bill eliminates the income tax on capital gains and dividends and repeals the estate and gift tax outright, while investment purchases are exempt from the replacement sales tax [S2][S3]. The revenue difference is made up by taxing consumption, which falls proportionally hardest on families that spend most of their income [S3].

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and defunding the IRS after fiscal 2009 eliminates the compliance burden — and the industry built on it — that millions of households pay for every year [S2].

industries.industry: Retailers and sellers of goods and services
industries.note: Every seller of taxable property or services becomes a required collector of the federal sales tax, with monthly reporting, segregated tax accounts, bond requirements for large sellers, and penalties for failure to remit [S3]. In exchange, sellers get an administrative credit of at least $200 or 0.25 percent of tax remitted, making them a permanently paid arm of federal tax collection [S3].

industries.industry: State governments with existing sales taxes
industries.note: States that agree to collect the federal tax may keep a 0.25 percent administration fee and gain a large new federal role in tax administration [S2][S3].
Financial intermediation services — bank and financial fees — become taxable under the new sales tax, a new levy on services that were not directly taxed under the income tax system [S3].
